title: The Future's Bright
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison, writing as a head teacher, describes an after-school session in which Year 2 Early Career Teachers (ECTs) presented their self-directed teaching improvement projects, demonstrating sophisticated reflective practice only a few months into the profession. Each ECT had chosen a specific instructional target -- Do Nows, cold calling pause time, mini-whiteboard routines, participation ratio, I-We-You modelling, programming scaffolds, vocabulary instruction -- and had implemented and assessed a discrete change rather than a vague improvement goal. Allison's framing is optimistic: this generation of new teachers is entering the profession with principled, evidence-informed approaches and the professional humility to test and adjust them. The piece is notable as a counterpoint to doom narratives about teacher recruitment and retention, offering instead a snapshot of what early-career professional development looks like when it is grounded in classroom evidence rather than top-down compliance.
points: * Each ECT chose one narrow, measurable instructional target -- one student changed only the timing of her cold-call pause, another changed only the transition signal for mini-whiteboards -- which allowed them to attribute observed effects to the intervention rather than confounding variables. * Buce's cold-call pause-time fix ('1, 2, 3, 4 -- I need to wait a little more,' said internally) is a concrete self-regulation strategy for a common problem: teachers consistently underestimate how long they actually wait before redirecting the question to a named student. * Tom's response to students writing '?' or 'IDK' on mini-whiteboards -- requiring them to put boards down and write an attempt -- is a direct structural fix to the participation-ratio problem, converting opt-out tools into mandatory engagement prompts. * Ed's use of student survey data after several weeks of exam-question Do Nows -- asking students about challenge level, confidence, and accuracy -- introduces a metacognitive layer: students reflecting on their learning experience as part of the instructional cycle. * Zara's I-We-You modelling approach illustrates the importance of compliance check before the 'You' stage -- using mini-whiteboards to assess understanding before releasing students to independent work, rather than assuming readiness from behavioral compliance alone.
quotes: Georgina (maths) had been reflecting on her 'Do Nows'. She wanted to make sure she was making the most of them. With this in mind, as students were working on the 'Do Now' questions, she would circulate and look at their responses. She would spot any common errors and misconceptions and make a note of them.

Buce made one simple change to her cold-call questioning. After asking a question, she would say (in her head), '1, 2, 3, 4 -- I need to wait a little more,' before directing the question at a named student. This made her leave a longer pause between the question and the student name.

Tom made a change: if students did this, he asked them to put their boards down and write an answer -- even if they weren't sure. This has resulted in more students participating first time and, as a result, is giving Tom a better understanding of how the whole class is doing.

Ed started using past exam questions for them. After a few weeks of doing this with Year 10, he asked students to complete a survey on their experience. By encouraging students to reflect on their learning experience, Ed is hoping to develop them as metacognitive learners.

Before moving on to the 'you' stage of independent practice, Zara uses MWBs to gauge understanding. This allows her to identify if further support is needed before students begin their independent work.

David has explicitly taught the PRIMM staged approach to solving a programming problem (Predict > Run > Investigate > Modify > Make). This has provided students with a framework to scaffold their thinking by breaking complex tasks down into smaller, achievable steps.
Each of them shared an aspect of their teaching they had been focusing on and how this was going. I was so impressed with their reflective, honest, and precise approach to this.
